claims.text: Adding an intermediate thermal dwell enhances precursor equilibration.
The intermediate dwell produces uniform pre-nucleation clusters or mobile intermediate species.
Uniform pre-nucleation clusters cause the constituent metals to nucleate simultaneously.
Simultaneous nucleation promotes formation of a single-phase solid solution.
Locally well-mixed solid noble-metal precursors can yield single-phase HEA nanoparticles upon thermal decomposition and reduction.
A dwell at approximately 150–200 °C for 5–15 minutes is an appropriate intervention before final rapid heating.
An inert or controlled atmosphere during the dwell prevents oxidation.
The proposed dwell favors partial precursor decomposition without causing premature nucleation.
Differences in reduction or decomposition kinetics among metal precursors create uneven atomic mobility during rapid heating.
Uneven or limited atomic mobility can contribute to local elemental segregation and structure selection.
The dwell increases diffusion and brings all metal species to a similar degree of equilibration before final heating.
Relative to direct rapid heating, the dwell-treated particles will show sharper, singular X-ray diffraction peaks indicating a single phase.
Relative to direct rapid heating, the dwell-treated particles will have a more uniform elemental distribution.
Relative to direct rapid heating, the dwell-treated particles will have more homogeneous particle morphology.
The dwell-treated material will have a lower apparent decomposition-onset temperature.
Direct rapid heating and cooling typically produces multiple phases, elemental segregation, and heterogeneous particle morphology because precursor reduction is nonuniform.
The mechanism applies to Pt–Pd–Rh–Ir–Au systems, optionally containing Ru, within a 150–200 °C and 5–15 minute dwell window.
Dwell conditions outside the stated window may cause premature nucleation or particle coarsening.
The optimal dwell temperature and time depend on precursor chemistry and loading.
